June 25, 1895.
SPECIAL ORDER UNDER GENERAL RULE III.
So much of Executive orders heretofore issued under General Rule III, section 2,
clause (c), as provides for the appointment of engineers and assistant engineers by
noncompetitive examination is hereby revoked, and hereafter engineers and assistant
engineers will be appointed by competitive examination.
Approved.
Grover Cleveland.
Executive Mansion, June 25, 1895.
July 11, 1895.
AMENDMENT TO CUSTOMS RULE V.
In the exercise of the power vested in him by the Constitution, by the seventeen
hundred and fifty-third section of the Revised Statutes, and the act entitled “An
act to regulate and improve the civil service of the United States,” approved Janu¬
ary 16, 1883, the President hereby makes and promulgates the following rule to can¬
cel and be in lieu of Customs Rule V of the revised civil-service rules:
Customs Rule V.
1. Until promotion regulations have been applied to a classified customs district the
following promotions may be made therein at any time after absolute appointment:
(a) Any employee in any grade, upon any test of fitness determined upon by the
nominating officer, to any vacant place in the class next above the one in which he
may be serving, except to the positions of weigher and gauger.
(b) Any employee in any grade may be promoted or transferred to a vacancy in
the lowest class of the grade of examiner after passing the examiner examination, to
a vacancy in the lowest class of the grade of weigher after passing the weigher exam¬
ination, to a vacancy in the lowest class of the grade of gauger after passing the
gauger examination, or to a vacancy in the lowest class of any other grade than the
one in which he may be serving upon passing the examination provided for that
grade.
Approved July 11, 1895.
Grover Cleveland.
July 15, 1895.
AMENDMENT TO DEPARTMENTAL RULE II.
Section 3, providing for exceptions from examinations in the classified Departmen¬
tal Service, is hereby amended as follows by the insertion of clause (g):
One designated clerk at each pension agency (designated to sign official checks for
the pension agent).
Section 4 is hereby amended as follows: On the third line, after the word “exam¬
ination,” add the following proviso:
Provided, That any person employed in an excepted place in any office or bureau at
the time when said office or bureau is brought into the classified service, or any per¬
son transferred directly from a nonexcepted to an excepted place in the office or
bureau in which he is serving, may, at any time, be directly transferred from such
excepted place to any nonexcepted place in the office or bureau in which he is
serving.
The section as amended will read:

made by any departmental rule shall be transferred from such place to a place not

EXECUTIVE ORDERS.
Navy-Yard Service.
The regulations of the Navy Department governing the employment of labor at
navy-yards having been adopted by the Civil Service Commission as a regulation of

the Revised Civil Service Rules of May 6, 1896, it is hereby ordered that no modifi¬

Philippine Service.
The United States Civil Service Commission is directed to render such assistance

Veteran Preference.
The attention of the Departments is hereby called to the provisions of the laws
giving preference to veterans in appointment and retention.
The President desires that wherever the needs of the service will justify it, and
the law will permit, preference shall be given alike in appointment and retention to
honorably discharged veterans of the civil war who are fit and well qualified to
perform the duties of the places which they seek or are filling.
Theodore Roosevelt.
White House, January 17, 1902.
Attempts op Employees to Influence Legislation.
All officers and employees of the United States of every description, serving in
or under any of the Executive Departments, and whether so serving in or out of
Washington, are hereby forbidden, either directly or indirectly, individually or
through associations, to solicit an increase of pay or to influence or attempt to influ¬
ence in their own interest any other legislation whatever, either before Congress or
its committees, or in any way save through the heads of the Departments in or
under which they serve, on penalty of dismissal from the Government service.
Theodore Roosevelt.
White House, January SI, 1902.

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 141 
July 31, 1911. 
Mr. Thomas Richardson, who has been serving as postmaster at Port Gibson, Miss., since July 12, 1898, may be appointed to an appropriate position in the competitive classified service at Washington where his postal experience will be available, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil service rules. Investigation and report made to the satisfaction of the President shows the fitness of Mr. Richardson, after 15 years’ service in the Post Office Department, for the appointment at Washington in the competitive classified service. The commission recommends the issuance of the order. 
August 2, 1911. 
The provisions of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting Federal employees from holding office under any State, Territorial, or municipal government are hereby waived to permit Sylvester P. Bartlett, a field superintendent in the Bureau of Fisheries, to hold the position of secretary to the Illinois State Fish Com- mission, in view of the mutual advantages thereby secured to the State commission and the Bureau of Fisheries. This order is recommended by the Civil Service Com- mission. 
August 2, 1911. 
Charles B. Bateman may be transferred from the navy-yard service to any classified mechanical position in the departments at Washington for which his experience of 14 years as a machinist qualifies him. This order, which 1s concurred in by the Civil Service Commission, is issued in view of an unfortunate situation in which Mr. Bateman is shown to have been placed, and the fact being recognized that the good of the service is advanced by increasing the comfort and peacefulness, and hence the efficiency, of its working force. This matter is fully set forth in the commission’s letter of August 1, 1911. 
August 9, 1911. 
An appointment may be made to the position of secretary of the Interstate Com- merce Commission to succeed Mr. E. A. Moseley, who occupied this position from the date of its classification until his death, which recently occurred. The Inter- state Commerce Commission deems it desirable to appoint one who is not within the classified service, although in the employment of the commission. The Civil Service Commission joins in recommending this order. 
August 9, 1911. 
Mrs. Lilly Dent Rogers may be reinstated as a clerk of class 1 in the National Bank 
Redemption Agency in the Treasurer’s Office, Treasury Department, without regard to the length oF time since her separation from the service. Mrs. Rogers was a clerk in the Treasury Department from August 1, 1877, to June 30, 1888. She is the widow of the late Thomas E. Rogers, who was employed for nearly 37 years in the Treasurer’s Office and was superintendent of the National Bank Redemption Agency since April 6, 1883, the success of the agency having been due largely to his executive manage- ment and intelligent knowledge. The reinstatement of Mrs. Rogers is recommended by the Treasury Department, but not by the Civil Service Commission. 
August 9, 1911. 
Randolph Fortune, who served as assistant messenger and messenger in the War Department from September 4, 1890 to February 28, 1910, when he resigned to accept a position in the legislative service, may be reinstated to a messenger position in the ar Department without regard to the length of his separation from that department. The Adjutant General of the Army states that Mr. Fortune had a good record in that office in which he served many years. If Mr. Fortune had entered the competitive classified service through examination instead of by classification he would have*been eligible for retransfer under the civil service rules as amended on April 21, 1911. In view of all the facts in the case the commission joins the War Department in recom- mending the issuance of the order. 
August 21, 1911. 
Mr. Norris R. Welsh, a skilled laborer in the Government Printing Office, at $780 per annum, may be transferred to a position in the Division of Publications, Department of Agriculture, at a salary of $720 per annum—a reduction of $60. This transfer has been requested by the Secretary of Agriculture for the reason that Mr. Welsh has a thorough knowledge of the publications of the Agricultural Depart- ment, and occupies a position in the Government Printing Office which peculiarly fits him for the position to which it is proposed to assign him, and that the transfer isin

The Civil Service Commission does not approve of the transfer of Mr. Welsh, on the ground that the transfer is an appointment within the meaning of the civil service act, and that a transfer from a nonapportioned to an apportioned service involves a charge to a district which has already received an excessive share of apportioned appoint- ments; and that the evidence submitted does not establish the fact that a man selected from the eligible list would not be just as satisfactory. 
August 22, 1911. 
Mr. Edwin L. Williams, formerly clerk to the Committee on the Post Office and Post Roads of the House of Representatives, may be appointed to a clerical position in the Post Office Department. This order is recommended by the Postmaster General, but not concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. Mr. Williams’ long service with the Committee on the Post Office and Post Roads has given him exceptional opportunity to become thoroughly familiar with the operations of the Post Office Department. This order is issued therefore because of his admitted experience and efficiency. 
October 2, 1911. 
Edwin M. Hamilton of New York may be appointed lumberman in the Indian Serv- ice at large, without reference to paragraph (a), civil service rule No. IX, relating to reinstatement, he having resigned February 28, 1909, from the position of supervisor in the Forest Service, in charge of the Black Hills National Park, with headquarters at Deadwood, S. Dak. June 11, 1912. 
Mrs. May Stanley may be appointed to a position in the classified service without examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Stanley is the widow of Will H. Stanley, superintendent of the Soboba Indian School, California, who was murdered May 3, 1912, by an Indian under the juris- diction of that superintendency. Mr. Stanley left two dependent children. Mrs. Stanley has been employed for several years in excepted positions in the Indian Service. She attended Dickinson County High School, Kansas, the Lebanon Val- ley College, Pennsylvania, and the University of Kansas, and the department believes that she will render efficient service in the capacity of teacher. In view of the facts the Civil Service Commission joins with the department in recommending the issuance of an Executive order. 
June 15, 1912. 
Mr. Oscar Wenderoth may be reinstated in the classified service to the position of Supervising Architect without regard to the length of time that he has been sepa- rated from the service. 
Mr. Wenderoth served as senior architectural draftsman and foreman of construction - in and under the Office of the Supervising Architect, from March 8, 1897, when he was appointed through appropriate examination, to April 16, 1900, when he resigned; and again from March 10, 1903, when he was reinstated by Executive order as senior architectural draftsman, to July 31, 1904. 
In view of his previous service, his experience, and his proved efficiency, the commission joins with the Secretary of the Treasury in recommending this order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. M. M. Dodge may be transferred, before the completion of his probationary 
period, from the position of clerk in the War Department to naturalization examiner at Pittsburgh, Pa. : 
The transfer of Mr. Dodge was desired by the department because of his high edu- cational attainments, mature judgment, and experience in law and in administrative matters. Mr. Dodge is regarded by the Division of Naturalization as peculiarly fitted for the duties of the position at Pittsburgh to which he is to be transferred. Under the civil-service rules an employee is not eligible for transfer from one depart- ment to another until he has served for six months and has received absolute appoint￾ment, and the Civil Service Commission was unable to concur with the department in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
June 19, 1912. 
Mr. John G. Lerch may be Spoil without examination as private secretary to Mr. lugene G. Hay, member of the Board of General Appraisers. The position is one of a highly confidential nature, as the secretary to the general appraiser must of necessity know in many instances in advance of the promulgation of decisions what the decisions will be. 
Mr. Lerch has had considerable previous experience in the capacity of secretary and has passed the civil-service examination in stenography and typewriting. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation for an Executive order. 
July 10, 1912. 
Mr. Leroy A. McGee may be reinstated to the position of post-office inspector without reference to the time limit upon eligibility for reinstatement. 
Mr. McGee served for four years as a teacher in the Indian Service, for three years as a clerk in the Office of the Auditor for the Post Office Department, and three years as a post-office inspector, resigning from the latter position on October 7, 1910. He has passed the teacher examination, the post-office inspector examination, and the immigrant inspector examination with good ratings. The chief post-office inspector reports that he was a good inspector, that his work was satisfactory, that there is nothing in the files which would be considered against his reinstatement, and that since his resignation Mr. McGee has been practicing law. In view of his good record and the fact that his experience since leaving the service has been such as to increase his efficiency, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Postmaster General in recom- mending the reinstatement,

The following-named employees of the Tariff Board who have been especially recom- mended for retention in the public service may be transferred or appointed to appro- riate positions in the competitive classified service with the approval of the Civil A, Commission; but in the case of any such person who has not a competitive status or who has not passed an appropriate examination for the position to which

Ingold, Mr. James Otey, Mr. Wilson Evans, Mr. Travers Pinn, Mr. J. Garfield Harris. Eligibility under this order shall cease at the expiration of one year from the date of the person’s separation from the Tariff Board. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the chairman of the Tariff Board, with the approval of the Civil Service Commission, on account of the faithful and meritorious service of the employees, most of whom have had considerable experience in the Government service, although not in all cases in the classified service, but in - no case less than 18 months. 
July 19, 1912. 
Mr. Dorsey E. Phillips, of Missouri, may be appointed to a clerical position in the competitive classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Phillips served for five years in the Regular Army prior to May 30, 1898. He passed the clerk examination held at St. Joseph, Mo., on March 22, 1909, with a rating of 78.35 and was temporarily employed as a result of this examination from October 25, 1909, to Feb- ruary 18, 1910. He also passed the census-clerk examination with a rating of 80.25, as a result of which he received appointment in the Bureau of the Census and served from September 6, 1910, to February 29, 1912, when he was separated on account of a necessary reduction of force. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the approval of this order. 
July 23, 1912. 
Mr. Isaac D. Laferty may be reinstated in the Bureau of Pensions, Department of the Interior, without reference to the time limit of eligibility for reinstatement under the civil-service rules. Mr. Laferty was appointed to a clerical position in the Pension Office on August 11,

REPORT OF UNITED STATES CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 139 
The opinion of the President conveyed in the letter of his Secretary will be treated as an Executive order. (Minute 1, Mar. 23, 1912.) 
PETITIONS TO CONGRESS BY CIVIL-SERVICE EMPLOYEES, 
April 8, 1912.1 
It is hereby ordered that petitions or other communications regarding public busi- ness addressed to Congress or either House or any committee or Member thereof by officers or employees in the civil service of the United States shall be transmitted through the heads of their respective departments or offices, who shall forward them without delay with such comment as they may deem requisite in the public interest. Officers and employees are strictly prohibited either directly or indirectly from at- tempting to secure legislation, or to influence pending legislation, except in the manner above prescribed. This order supersedes the Executive orders of January 31, 1902, January 25, 1906, and November 26, 1909, regarding the same general matter 
EXCEPTIONS IN MACHINE SHOP OF THE BUREAU OF THE CENSUS. 
August 21, 1812. - 
With a view to meeting emergencies in the machine shop of the Bureau of the Census, in connection with the continuation of the Thirteenth Decennial Census work during the fiscal year 1913, the Secretary of Commerce and Labor is hereby authorized to employ, until June 30, 1913, without reference to the civil-service rules, such machinists, toolmakers, electricians, and apprentice boys (machinists) as may be necessary for the prosecution of the work whenever, in his opinion, it is not prac- ticable to make such appointments from the civil-service lists. This order extends the authority for similar appointments contained in the Executive order of December 29, 1909. The Civil Service Commission concurs with the department in recommending this order, in view of the representations of the department as to its necessity. ! 
EMPLOYMENT IN PENSION OFFICE OF FORMER TREASURY EMPLOYEES. 
August 24, 1912. 
The Commissioner of Pensions is directed to employ as extra clerks under the appro- priation of $300,000 carried in the sundry civil act approved August 24, 1912, the 30 persons heretofore employed in the office of the Auditor for the Post Office Depart- ment whose names are on the list furnished to the President in a letter of the Secre- tary of the Treasury dated August 22, 1912, said appropriation act authorizing the Commissioner of Pensions to employ clerks heretofore employed in other departments of the Government service. All of these persons except one have a competitive classified status and will be eligible for reinstatement in the Treasury Department under the civil-service rules. 
MODERATOR OF A TOWN MEETING MAY BE A CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEE, 
August 24, 1912. 
The temporary office of moderator of a town meeting and offices of a like character are hereby excepted from the operation of the Executive order of January 17, 1873, prohibiting persons in the Federal civil service from holding office under the charter or ordinances of any municipal corporation, and may be held by persons in the execu- tive civil service. Membership in the civil service ought not to prevent an employee from taking part in the ordinary municipal affairs of the community in which he lives, where that part does not involve permanent service but only such a temporary duty as that of acting as chairman of a municipal business meeting, where such service is not compensated by any salary or other emolument, and where the attention required by such service does not interfere with the regular and efficient discharge of the duties of the Federal office held. In the exercise of the privilege granted by this order officers and employees must not neglect their official duties and must not engage in national, State, or county political activity in violation of the civil-service rules; and in seeking the local offices named or in performing the duties thereof employees shall not use the authority or influence of their Federal positions nor take an active part in political management or 
 
in political campaigns.

CLASSIFICATION OF POSITION OF SPECIAL EMPLOYEE, INTERNAL-REVENUE SERVICE. 
August 24, 1912. 
The position of special employee in the Internal-Revenue Service shall hereafter be regarded as classified under the civil-service act and rules. No such special employee now serving shall be regarded as classified hereunder or shall acquire any right of promotion or transfer under the rules unless he is specially commended therefor by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, with the approval of the Secretary of the Treasury, because of efficient services rendered, and whose name is embraced in the is furnished to the Civil Service Commission by the Treasury Department of this 
ate. The Treasury Department may make appointments of special employees for a period not exceeding 30 days or not exceeding 45 days in any one quarter of any fiscal year without reference to the civil-service rules. This order shall take effect October 1, 1912, and is issued with the concurrence of the Secretary of the Treasury and the Civil Service Commission. 
CLASSIFICATION AUTHORIZED OF CERTAIN EXPERTS IN THE DEPARTMENT OF AGRI- CULTURE. August 26, 1912. 
Not exceeding 115 persons appointed as experts and agents without examination under Subdivision IX, section 1 of Schedule A, of the civil-service rules, and who now are engaged upon work similar to that of competitive employees, and who are especially recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture because of their proved capacity for efficient service may be transferred to appropriate competitive positions in the Department of Agriculture. By Executive order of this date the provision of the civil-service rules permitting the appointment of agents and experts of the Department of Agriculture without examination is amended to fix more definitely the conditions under which appoint- ments can be made. This order will thus permit the classification of efficient em- ployees who can not be properly regarded as agents or experts under the amended procedure. Many of these persons are college graduates and, having been appointed at a time when agricultural colleges had not developed courses of study along certain technical lines pursued by the department, have become technologists and experts while engaged in the work of the department. The Civil Service Commission recommends this order.

Office of Indian Affairs, the requirement of the civil service rule relative to reinstate- ment being hereby waived, it appearing that Mrs. Clark was a classified employee in the Indian Service until June 31, 1906. This order is recommended by the Secretary 
of the Interior and concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. 
September 2, 1912. 
Mr. G. M. Davison may be reinstated as storekeeper-gauger in the Internal-Revenue Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Davison was storekeeper-gauger for several years, his final separation from that service having occurred by resignation on July 5, 1893. He subsequently served as assistant United States attorney for more than nine years, attending six courts and prosecuting at least 350 cases a year for violation of the internal-revenue laws. It appears that while in this service by reason of overwork and exposure in severe winter weather he was stricken with dropsical and muscular rheumatism. The Secretary of the Treasury approves the recommendation of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue that his reinstatement be permitted by Executive order and in view of the facts the Civil 
Service Commission also concurs in the recommendation. 
September 7, 1912. 
Mr. James B. Brunemer may be appointed a watchman in the Government Printing Office. He is a veteran of the Civil War and served as a watchman in the Post Office Department and later as a clerk in the Treasury and Interior Departments. He is eligible for reinstatement under the rules in any of these departments because of his former service therein; but not in the Government Printing Office. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Public Printer, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission, as there are no eligible applicants among the veterans employed in the Government Printing Office. This action merely permits reinstate- ment in an office other than one for which the applicant is already eligible. 
September 7, 1912. 
Miss Mabel Hiatt may be appointed to a clerical position in the Department of Agriculture without reference to the civil service rules. This order is recommended by the Secretary of Agriculture, but is not concurred in by the Civil Service Commis￾gion. 
September 17, 1912. : 
Mr. George S. Livingston may be reinstated to an appropriate position in the Pension Office without regard to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Livingston 
entered the Government service on October 1, 1888, by classification, and was removed on October 31, 1905, from the Pension Office because of his connection with a money- lending association. In view of the needs of the service and of the definite recommendation of the Sec- retary of the Interior and the Commissioner of Pensions, and of the statement of the Commissioner of Pensions that Mr. Livingston was undoubtedly too severely punished for the slight unintentional offense given by him, the Civil Service Commission joins in the recommendation for an order permitting his reinstatement.

Mr. R. A. Kirk may be appointed a deputy collector of internal revenue without

concur in the issuance of this order.

George E. Long may be promoted from the position of messenger to a minor clerical osition in the Bureau of Insular Affairs of the War Department without examination. his order is made upon the recommendation of the Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs on account of Mr. Long’s long service and unusual record, and is approved by the War Department and the Civil Service Commission. : 
September 30, 1912. 
George Ii. Long may be promoted from the position of messenger to a clerkship of the lowest class in the Bureau of Insular Affairs of the War Department without 
examination.

October 4, 1912. 
Mr. John XK. Robinson may be reinstated as a printer in the Weather Bureau with- out reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Robinson was an enlisted man and noncommissioned officer of the Signal Corps of the Army for a number of years, and when the meteorological division of the Signal Corps became a part of the Weather Bureau he was transferred to the Weather Bureau and remained for several years, when he was discharged on false charges without proper opportunity to defend himself. 
The Acting Secretary of Agriculture and the Civil Service Commission recommend the reinstatement. 
APPOINTMENTS AUTHORIZED, WITHOUT COMPETITION, 
UNDER EXECUTIVE ORDER OF DECEMBER 1, 1910. 
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE. 
Dr. Frank J. Loomis as veterinary inspector. (Minute 1, July 24, 1912.) 
Dr. Loomis was appointed as a veterinary inspector at Watertown, N. Y., to be paid at the rate of $5 per diem when actually employed, not to exceed $300 per annum, under Schedule A of the civil service rules. He passed the veterinary inspector examination and was certified and offered appointment, but declined. The depart- ment desired to readjust the quarantine work along the Canadian boundary and to extend Dr. Loomis’s territory to cover Ogdensburg, N. Y., which would require a greater number of days’ employment. Authority was requested to increase his com- pensation not to exceed $800 in any fiscal year. It was claimed that the work was of such an intermittent nature that it would not justify the appointment of a regular inspector and that Dr. Loomis was a practicing veterinarian at Watertown, N. Y., I could handle the work without detriment to his private practice.

A. Lincoln Dryden as navigation officer, at $1,200 per annum. (Minute 1, May 17, 
1912.) 
The appointment of A. Lincoln Dryden was desired in order that he might take charge of the motor boat purchased by the department in connection with the enforce- ment of the navigation laws on Chesapeake Bay and its tributaries and connecting 
waters. sioners of the District of Columbia and bears an excellent testimonial. The Depart- ment of Agriculture reports that the department ‘would be glad to place him in the department, as he is a clean, reliable sort of man.” The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of this order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Fred Roege may be reinstated as assistant postmaster in the post office at Pen- sacola, Fla., without regard to the length of time that he has been separated from the service. Mr. Roege was appointed to the classified service on August 28, 1900, and served con￾tinuously till July 13, 1911, when he resigned. He held the position of clerk in the Treasury Department, money-order clerk in the Washington post office, and post- office inspector. He made application for reinstatement within the year of his eligi￾bility, but was misinformed to the effect that his military service and honorable discharge therefrom rendered him eligible for reinstatement at any time under the rules. In view of the fact that he was misinformed as to his rights of reinstatement the com- mission concurs in the recommendation of the Postmaster General, the First Assistant Postmaster General, and the postmaster at Pensacola that he be reinstated by ex- ecutive order. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Charles H. Shaw, now employed in the Customs Service at the port of New York, may be appointed to a classified position in the New York customs service without reference to the civil-service rules. This appointment is recommended by the collector of the port of New York and the Secretary of the Treasury, but is not concurred in by the Civil Service Commission. It appears from the papers in the case that Mr. Shaw who is a lawyer, had been employed from July 1, 1909, in the customhouse in an unclassified position on the “fraud roll;” that he had rendered most excellent service, and that the collector recommended the order as one distinctly in the interests of the service. 
March 3, 1913. 
Mr. Jesse L. Suter may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Suter was appointed confidential clerk at $1,800 per annum in the office of the First Assistant Postmaster General on August 9, 1909, the position being excepted from examination under Schedule A of the civil-service rules. The Postmaster Gen- eral states that Mr. Suter, since his appointment, has qualified himself in an excep- tional manner for usefulness in the department; that he is a man of college education, and trained in journalism, for which reason he has been assigned to editorial work, and that in the course of his duties he has familiarized himself with the operations of all branches of the postal service. As the staff of men in the department competent to do editorial work with expert knowledge of the subject matter is limited, the Post- master General is of the opinion that it will be of decided ad vantage to the Government to have Mr. Suter continue in the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
March 10, 1918. 
Mrs. Mabel P. LeRoy, of Michigan, appointed by the Secretary of the Interior February 26, 1910, to the position of clerk to sign land patents, is hereby designated as required by law to sign said patents.

Mr. Edward H. Hayden may be appointed to any position in the classified civil 
service of the Treasury Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. This order was issued on the statement of the Secretary of the Treasury that he deemed it important that he should have in addition to his private secretary and stenographer, a confidential clerk attached to his immediate staff in whom he had 
complete confidence. He stated that he was unable to find any one in the classified service who could meet this peculiar need. : 
April 21, 1913. 
Mr. Theodore T. Kirk may be appointed to the position of assistant mechanical draftsman in the Navy Department. Mr. Kirk was appointed a teacher in the Philippine service through examination on August 27, 1907, and served to May 28, 1910. If he had served to August 27, 1910, his reinstatement and transfer would be permissible under existing rules. Since his separation from the Philippine service he has served one year and seven months as junior engineer temporarily in the Bureau of Mines. He passed an examination for surveyor for the Philippine service, and an examination for mechanical draftsman
